_why: The single source of truth for what a sprite in this game is. Everything in
the pipeline reads this file: the generator prompts, the normaliser, the
validator, the proposals page and the Godot importer. Hand-copied numbers
rot -- the belt speed changed by a factor of ten while three doc pages went
on quoting the old value -- and a sprite spec that has drifted produces art
that is subtly wrong in a way nobody can point at.
The measurement that produced these numbers: the game currently draws a
300-pixel illustration of the player at 20x31 game pixels, a 0.105 downscale
with a nearest filter and no mipmaps. That means the renderer keeps one
source pixel in ninety and throws the rest away, and *which* one it keeps
depends on the character's sub-pixel position. Thin details appear and
vanish between frames; the silhouette itself changes when the character
moves half a pixel. That is the shimmer this repository has recorded twice
as an animation bug and tried to fix twice at the anchor level.
So the rule underneath every number below is: stored resolution equals
displayed resolution. No downscale at draw time, therefore no sub-sampling,
therefore the whole class of problem is gone rather than mitigated.
64 rather than 32 so an action pose has somewhere to go: a mining swing
raises the arms above the head and a carried cat sits in front of the
chest, and both were cropped by a tight cell. The body occupies about
half the cell; the space above is for the pose and the space below is
for the shadow, which is drawn in-engine and must not be baked in.
The foot anchor is where the character touches the ground, and it is
the number that every frame is aligned to. It is not the cell centre.
Every number here is character doubled, and it exists to answer one
question before the game commits to a sprite size: what does the
generated footage actually contain, and how much of it survives the
reduction to 64? The source is 480p of a character about 530 pixels
tall, so 128 throws away far less than 64 does. Normalising the same
frames at both sizes and looking at them side by side is the only
honest way to see what the smaller cell costs.
An earlier version of this note said a 128 character would stand four
tiles tall and that adopting it meant re-cutting every tile. Both were
wrong, and worth leaving corrected here rather than quietly deleted.
The world is drawn procedurally -- 95 draw_rect and 90 draw_circle
calls, three PNGs in the whole game and all of them characters -- so
tiles have no resolution to match. And the cell does not set the
character's size in the world; the draw scale does. A 128 sheet drawn
at half scale occupies exactly the space a 64 sheet does at full.
What the cell actually decides is texels per logical pixel. The body
spans about 32 logical pixels and a 1920x1080 window is twice the
960x540 viewport, so 64 lands at 2x and shows its grid while 128 lands
at 1:1. 256 is the same argument for 4K.

_directions_why: Eight for the artwork; the game's build targeting stays on four cardinals
because belts and machine outputs are cardinal. The west-side frames are
mirrored from the east in-engine rather than drawn, which halves the
generation cost and makes left/right symmetry exact instead of nearly.
_animations_why: Eight frames at ten a second for every motion, deliberately uniform. The
counts used to differ per motion and bought nothing: a six-frame mine and
an eight-frame walk still have to be sampled across one full cycle, and the
sheet layout, the engine's frame arithmetic and the tests all get simpler
when there is one answer. What differs between motions is what happens
inside the cycle, not how many slots it is cut into.
_feet_planted_why: An idle is defined by the feet not moving. The cycle finder does not know
that -- it scores how well a window closes and how little it repeats -- so
on a four second clip of someone standing still it happily picked frames
where the character shifted her weight, and at six frames a second that
read as very slow walking. A person watching it said so immediately.
Measured on that clip: across all 48 frames the boots moved 140px, but the
steadiest eight-frame window moved 4px while the head still rose and fell
6px. The breathing was there the whole time, in a window the finder had no
reason to prefer. This flag makes the pipeline pick for planted feet first
and closure second, for the motions where standing still is the point.
_animation_area_why: mine also carries its own area tolerance, for the same reason and with the
same kind of evidence. A pickaxe entering and leaving the silhouette
changes how much of it there is, and by an order of magnitude more than a
stride does. Measured across finished sequences: walking and running change
area by at most 1% between frames, while the three mining directions change
by 9%, 9% and 13%. The front view is the largest because the tool swings
toward and away from the camera there, changing apparent size as well as
position. 0.20 clears the observed 13% without approaching anything a walk
_animation_jump_why: mine carries its own centroid tolerance because how much a silhouette may
change between two frames is a property of the motion, not of the game. A
pickaxe travels from above the head to the ground and back inside six
frames; the tool alone crosses roughly a body height in about three of
them, so the centre of the silhouette genuinely moves several pixels per
frame. Measured on a swing that was checked by eye first: 10.9px of a 64px
body, which is 0.17. 0.20 leaves room without inventing any.
It is per motion rather than a raised global limit because raising the
global limit was tried and is wrong. The two things that needed separating
were a real swing at 10.9px and a walk clip whose chroma key had failed,
leaving a background block drifting behind the character at 9.0px. Magnitude
alone cannot tell those apart -- and neither can any shape statistic, both
of which were measured: the faulty clip's detour ratio was 1.3, lower than
a clean run cycle's 3.2, because the block moved smoothly. What separates
them is that one is a swing and the other is a walk, and the spec already

_why: How tall a character is, in source pixels, measured once from clips where
its hands are empty. Every clip of that character normalises against this
number instead of against its own silhouette.
The mining sheets are why this exists. The normaliser sized each sequence
by the longest unbroken run of rows containing pixels, which it calls the
body -- and a raised pickaxe is held in the hands, so it is part of that
run. Measured across Grim's clips: walking 486, idling 482, side walk 480,
running 492, all within 2.5% of each other; the three mining clips
measured 530, 434 and 558. The pipeline dutifully scaled each of those to
the same cell height, so Grim grew 10% when she mined facing away and
shrank 15% when she mined to the side. A player watching it said she got
smaller when she started mining, which is exactly what happened.
Note the cell did not need to change. The character128 anchor puts the
feet at y=104, leaving 104 pixels above them for a body of about 64 -- a
raised tool at a fixed scale reaches 74 and fits with room to spare. The
problem was never that the tool had nowhere to go; it was that the tool
was being counted as part of the character.
_when_it_applies: Only to motions marked carries_tool. Everywhere else the clip's own
measurement is better, and applying this to all of them was a mistake
worth writing down. The generator does not draw a character at exactly
one size across clips -- Grim came out 480 to 492 and the cat 573 to 640
-- and measuring each clip is what absorbs that: each one is scaled so
the character lands on the cell's body height, whatever it started at.
Forcing a shared number instead *reintroduces* the drift. The standing
cat, whose clip is 640 and which was told it was 595, rendered 7.5%
larger than the walking one, and it was visible in the game.
So the rule is narrow: use this when the measurement includes something
that is not the character, and only then.
_catorg_why: 595 is the median of the three walking clips (595, 595, 573). The idle
clip measures 640, which is the full height of the frame -- the keying
leaves something touching both edges there, so its own measurement is not
the cat. Sizing it against the walks is what keeps a standing cat the same

_palette_why: A locked palette is the cheapest consistency check there is. Drift that is
invisible in a 24-bit image -- a highlight two units warmer than it was in
the previous frame -- becomes a hard failure the moment the only legal
colours are these. It is also what makes a generated frame and a
hand-touched frame belong to the same game.
Sampled from Defs.gd so the sprites and the drawn machines cannot disagree.

_palette_families.world: Defs.gd -- the machines, the UI and the ground. Sprites and drawn objects must not disagree about what this game's colours are.
_why: The world colours alone were not enough and the pipeline said so on its
first real run: quantising the existing character against them turned
auburn hair near-black, because nothing in the machine palette is a warm
dark red. These three ramps are sampled from the shipped character art
-- the families that actually cover it, not invented ones -- so the
character stays the character while still being unable to drift.

_alpha_why: Sprites are hard-edged: a pixel is either in the sprite or it is not.
Semi-transparent edges are what make a nearest-filtered sprite look like a
photograph of a sprite, and they defeat the silhouette measurement the
validator uses to check that a character is not wobbling.

_max_centroid_jump_why: A fraction of the body height, not a pixel count, because the same motion
measures twice as far in a cell twice as large. This was 3.0 absolute
pixels, chosen when 64 was the only cell; adding character128 silently
halved the tolerance and rejected sequences that had passed. 0.094 of the
body height is 3.0px at 64 and 6.0px at 128 -- the same rule, stated in a
way that survives a change of cell.
Deliberately still an absolute ceiling rather than a multiple of the
sequence's own median jump. That alternative was measured and is worse:
on a clip where a failed chroma key left a background block wobbling
behind the character every single frame, the jumps were uniformly large,
so the ratio to the median came out 1.6 -- lower than a clean run cycle's
2.3. A rule that compares a sequence against itself cannot see a fault
_why: Half a pixel, and not because half a pixel of slop is acceptable. The foot
is the mean of the sprite's bottom row, so on a bottom row of even width
it lands between two pixels, and no integer placement can put it exactly
on the anchor. 0.5 is the grid's own quantisation. Anything above it is
the normaliser failing to place the sprite, which is a bug rather than a
tolerance -- the first run of this pipeline reported 0.5 and that is how
the distinction got found. The centroid and area limits
catch the failure this repository actually hit: frames that are each
individually fine but do not belong to the same walk cycle, so the
character's mass jumps around between them. The area limit was 0.25 and
let a 21% jump through -- a frame the eye caught at a glance on the
proposals page. With one shared scale across a sequence the real spread
is a few percent, so 0.12 is loose enough for a pose and tight enough to
catch a character resizing. Numbers are per adjacent
frame pair, not against the first frame -- a cycle is allowed to travel,
it is not allowed to jerk.
